solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: After payment, back versatile public transport

indicators.note: to go back is to run the other way, so the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: POST is the Latin-derived prefix meaning after
a sub is a subscription, a regular payment

explanation.surface: Someone praises a flexible transport system as worth backing once the fare is paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After payment' reads as a time phrase, but both words give letters. A sub is short for subscription, a regular fee.
explanation.definitionFit: A postbus is a rural mail van in Britain that also carries passengers, so it serves two purposes as a flexible kind of service.

clue.text: Gut feeling about West Ham after a year

indicators.note: in the East London accent of West Ham an initial H is dropped, so the word is spoken without its first letter

blocks.note: p.a. is per annum, Latin for a year
a hunch is an intuitive feeling

explanation.surface: A football fan has had a gut feeling about West Ham, the London club, for a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gut feeling' looks like one phrase, but Gut is the definition. West Ham is a football club in East London, where Cockney speech drops the H at the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: A paunch is a large protruding belly, and gut is an informal word for the same stomach area.

clue.text: Surpass what singers do in TV land

definitions.note: a verb phrase: go beyond merely singeing

blocks.note: a TV is a television set
to alight is to land, as a bird does on a branch

explanation.surface: Talent-show contestants on television are urged to outdo what other vocalists manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singers' are not vocalists but things that singe. Singeing is only light scorching, so going further than a singer does means making something burn outright.
explanation.definitionFit: To scorch something is less than to start it burning, so exceeding a scorch amounts to kindling a real fire.

clue.text: Work meeting getting Swede upset and cross

indicators.note: something upset is turned over, and in a down entry that puts its letters in the opposite order

blocks.note: a bee is a gathering for shared work, as in a sewing bee
Olaf is a typical Scandinavian first name, standing for any Swede

explanation.surface: An office meeting leaves a Swedish colleague upset and angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective for the upset Swede, but it is a noun: a hybrid animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A beefalo is a hybrid bred from domestic cattle and American bison, and a cross is the offspring of two different breeds.

clue.text: Rogue whose dad’s loaded?

blocks.note: first meaning: an old affectionate term for a rascal
second meaning, read literally: a child whose father is a firearm, and a firearm is loaded with bullets, not money

explanation.surface: A spoilt rascal can behave badly because his father is wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaded' means rich in the surface; read literally, it is what a weapon is when charged with ammunition, so the father is a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an old affectionate term for a scamp, and taken word by word it names the offspring of a firearm.

clue.text: Feeble desire to accommodate mischievous child

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to house them, so one piece takes another inside it

blocks.note: a wish is a desire
an imp is a mischievous child

explanation.surface: A weak longing to put up a naughty youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: The child goes in right after the first letter of the desire.
explanation.definitionFit: Wimpish describes someone weak and lacking courage, which matches feeble as an adjective of timid weakness.

clue.text: In place of whiskey, accept this

blocks.note: whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet
'here!' is said when handing something over for someone to take

explanation.surface: Someone is offered a substitute drink instead of the whisky they wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In place of' looks like one phrase meaning instead of; the definition is only 'In place', and 'of' joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The relative adverb introduces a location, as in the town where she lives, meaning the town in which place she lives.

clue.text: Coming in low, over cape, enormous bird. Hide!

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing over another sits above it, so it is written first
to come in is to enter, so the pair goes inside the other piece

blocks.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
the roc is a giant bird of Arabian legend
C is the map abbreviation for cape

explanation.surface: A huge bird swoops low over a headland, and someone shouts to take cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide!' reads as a command to take cover, but it is a noun for animal skin. In a down clue the bird sits over the cape, and both go inside the cow's sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Morocco is a fine goatskin leather used in bookbinding, and a hide is the skin of an animal.

clue.text: Shot of Russian composer dismissing notorious landlord

indicators.note: to dismiss is to send away, so part of the name is removed

blocks.note: Sergei Rachmaninoff, the Russian composer
Peter Rachman was a notoriously exploitative London slum landlord of the 1950s and 60s

explanation.surface: A photograph of a Russian composer throwing out a bad landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' suggests a photo or a drink; it is a billiards stroke. Rachman was so infamous that 'Rachmanism' became the British word for exploiting tenants.
explanation.definitionFit: In billiards and snooker an in-off is a stroke where the cue ball goes into a pocket after striking another ball.

clue.text: They save buckles for strapping

indicators.note: something that buckles bends out of shape, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: People keep the buckles to use on straps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buckles' and 'strapping' seem to belong together as harness fittings; buckles is a verb here, and strapping means burly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a person with a large, sturdy, powerfully built body.

clue.text: To increase demands at college, you must devour a lot of books

indicators.note: to devour is to swallow, so one piece ends up inside another

blocks.note: a British student is 'up' at university during term
thee is the old form of you
taken as written
NT is the New Testament, a collection of books

explanation.surface: A tutor tells a student that raising their standards means reading a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a student is 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge during term. The Bible's New Testament is a collection of many books.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from poker, where raising the stake means players must pay more, so it now means making stiffer requirements.

clue.text: Games host recently in Germany agreed to supply wine

blocks.note: Rio de Janeiro hosted the 2016 Olympic Games
ja is German for yes

explanation.surface: A recent Olympic host city made a deal in Germany to provide wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Rio de Janeiro hosted the 2016 Olympics, and JA is the German for yes, the answer given by someone who has agreed.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioja is a red or white wine from the Spanish region of La Rioja.

clue.text: What are the odds of criminal receiving fifty lashes?

indicators.note: odds here are odd-numbered positions, so the first, third, fifth and seventh letters are kept
to receive something is to take it in, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: letters 1, 3, 5 and 7 of the word
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone asks the betting odds on an offender being sentenced to fifty strokes of the whip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lashes' suggests flogging; it means eyelashes. L goes into the middle of CIIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Cilia is the anatomical term for eyelashes, and lashes is the everyday short form of the same word.

clue.text: Nice way to do the part of King Edward?

definitions.text: Nice way to do the part of King Edward?

blocks.clueFragment: Nice way to do the part of King Edward?
blocks.note: surface reading: a fine way for an actor to play the role of an English king

blocks.clueFragment: Nice way to do the part of King Edward?
blocks.note: setter's reading: Nice is the city on the Riviera, King Edward is a potato variety, and 'do' means cook

explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised at the start, 'Nice' hides the French city; King Edward is a popular British variety of potato, and a piece of one cooked the way they do it in France is a chip.
explanation.definitionFit: A strip of potato deep-fried in oil is the classic way potatoes are cooked in France, hence the name for a chip.

clue.text: I duck three times eg prior to blow in the kisser

indicators.note: to blow things is to scatter them in the wind, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like O
the abbreviation eg written three times
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone flinches repeatedly before being punched in the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kisser' is slang for the mouth, which suits the punch; here it means a person who kisses. Georgie Porgie of the nursery rhyme kissed the girls and made them cry.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery rhyme character is famous for kissing girls and making them cry, so he is the rhyme's kisser.

clue.text: Doctor in tuxedo heading for wedding ball’s leaving mark

indicators.note: the heading of something is its top, so only the opening letter is taken
to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A doctor in a dinner jacket leaves a formal ball on the way to a wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ball' suggests a dance, but it is a musket ball or bullet, and its leaving mark is the hole where it comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: An exit wound is the injury where a bullet emerges from the body, the damage it causes on its way out.

clue.text: Dope about to cut tree close to house? That’s rich!

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so only the final letter is taken
a knife that cuts goes into something, so one piece is set inside the other

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information, as is dope
ca is circa, Latin for about
the oak is a tree
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone fumes that a fool plans to chop down a tree right by their home, calling it a bit rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's rich!' sounds like an indignant exclamation, but it describes the answer. Gen, like dope, is British slang for inside information.
explanation.definitionFit: Genoa cake is a heavy British fruit cake with almonds, so it is a rich food, a description often used of dense cakes.

clue.text: Let’s chuck the bag on the bus: it’s always the last resort

indicators.note: always means every time, so from each word in turn only its final letter is kept

blocks.clueFragment: Let’s chuck the bag on the bus: it’s
blocks.note: the final letter of each of the eight words

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker throws their luggage onto the coach, joking that this place is where you end up when all else fails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last resort' looks like the idiom for a final option; 'the last' is the selection signal. Skegness is a seaside holiday town on the Lincolnshire coast of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Skegness is a traditional English seaside holiday town, and a resort is a place people visit for holidays.

clue.text: Old refuse heap to burn in range in centre of study

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: ken is range of knowledge, as in beyond my ken
to itch is to burn with a desire or an irritating sensation
mid means middle or centre
a den is a private study room

explanation.surface: Burning an ancient rubbish pile on a stove in the middle of a study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' suggests a kitchen stove, which fits the answer's first word, but it means scope of knowledge.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaeologists use the term for a prehistoric mound of shells, bones and domestic waste, an ancient dump of discarded rubbish.

clue.text: Explain why old ladies perhaps should stop in

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so these pieces fill a space inside another

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a ladies is a toilet, and WC is a water closet; 'perhaps' marks it as one example
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a reason why elderly women ought to stay indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the ladies' is a public women's toilet, and 'perhaps' marks the water closet as one example of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal question asks for the reason something is so, the same request as asking someone to account for it.

clue.text: Irish girl packing make-up with variable speed

indicators.note: packing a case means filling it, so other pieces are put inside this one

blocks.note: y is a standard algebraic variable
mph, miles per hour, is a unit of speed
DNA is one's genetic make-up

explanation.surface: An Irish girl packs her cosmetics and drives at varying speeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' suggests cosmetics; it is genetic make-up. Dymphna is an uncommon name, so the wordplay has to be trusted.
explanation.definitionFit: Dymphna is an Irish female given name, after a seventh-century Irish saint, so it names a girl from Ireland.

clue.text: Frail, after time dressing for the outdoor life?

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; the definition describes how such people dress

indicators.note: after means following, so one piece is written behind the other

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
weedy means thin and weak

explanation.surface: Someone grown weak with age takes up clothing suited to country living.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: tweed is the rough wool of country clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweedy describes someone habitually wearing tweed, the rugged wool cloth associated with country pursuits like hunting and walking.

clue.text: Woman putting on black while husband’s putting on green?

definitions.text: Woman putting on black while husband’s putting on green?

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman wearing mourning clothes, as if her husband had died
setter's reading: the husband is alive, putting a ball on a golf course, and she is only abandoned for the day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' changes meaning between halves: first dressing in mourning black, then tapping a ball on a golf green.
explanation.definitionFit: The humorous term describes a wife left alone so often by a husband obsessed with golf that she seems bereaved.

clue.text: Plain to see on reflection where general obligation falls?

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror is back to front, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a general obligation is binding on all

explanation.surface: Thinking it over, it is obvious who bears a shared duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain to see' reads as the phrase for obvious; Plain is the definition and 'to see' joins it on.
explanation.definitionFit: A llano is a grassy treeless plain in South America, from the Spanish word for flat land.

clue.text: Whack idiot

blocks.note: first meaning: a share or portion, as in one's whack
second meaning: British slang for a fool

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a command to hit a fool; both words are nouns, a share and a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A divvy is informal for a dividend or share, as is one's whack, and in British slang it also means a stupid person.

clue.text: How Persian might go without train to the west

indicators.note: in an across entry, heading west means moving right to left, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: w/o is the abbreviation for without
to train a gun on something is to aim it

explanation.surface: A traveller from Iran might have to manage without the railway on the journey west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Persian' suggests a person from Persia, but it is the long-haired cat breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A Persian is a breed of cat, and miaow is the sound a cat makes.

clue.text: One visiting writer at ode?

indicators.note: a visitor stays inside someone else's house, so the answer sits within the words that follow

blocks.note: spans the end of one word, a whole word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A figure who calls on a poet while they compose verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the muse sits inside the words and also visits the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Greek muse of lyric and love poetry, who inspires poets as they compose.

clue.text: Victor and I felt that Peter should provide grant

blocks.note: Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet
ouch is what someone says when they feel a sudden pain
peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: Two men named Victor and Peter share feelings about who should hand out a subsidy.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor and Peter look like two people's names; one is a radio code letter and the other safecracker's slang.
explanation.definitionFit: To vouchsafe is to give or bestow something graciously, a formal synonym of the verb to grant.

clue.text: Eccentric whose line is far from fine

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre and odd, so the letters are put into an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: An oddball whose remarks are anything but acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' suggests acceptable or delicate; it is fine weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Weather with frequent rain showers is the opposite of fine, dry, sunny weather.

clue.text: Play with funny bits of dull packaging poorly made

indicators.note: something done poorly is done badly, so the letters come out jumbled
packaging wraps around its contents, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: dry means dull and uninteresting
taken as written

explanation.surface: A child plays with amusing scraps of boring, cheaply made packaging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play with' looks like a verb phrase about toying with something; play is a noun, a drama.
explanation.definitionFit: A dramedy blends drama with comedy, so it is a serious play containing comic moments.
